questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: On a 64-bit system where `sizeof(int) = 4`, `sizeof(double) = 8`, and `sizeof(char) = 1`, what is `sizeof(union U)` for `union U { char c; int i; double d; };`?
questions.explanationEn: All members of a C `union` share the same starting memory address, so the size of a union equals the size of its largest member (padded to its alignment requirement): `max(1, 4, 8) = 8` bytes.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: In a 0-indexed array representation of a binary max-heap, what is the array index of the right child of the node stored at index `i`?
questions.explanationEn: For 0-based indexing, root is at 0, its children are at 1 and 2, and in general node `i` has left child `2i + 1` and right child `2i + 2`.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: In a binary tree, the preorder traversal is `A B D E C F` and the inorder traversal is `D B E A C F`. How many nodes are in the right subtree of the root `A`?
questions.explanationEn: From preorder, `A` is the root. In inorder `D B E | A | C F`, the nodes to the right of `A` are `C` and `F`, giving 2 nodes in the right subtree.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following output sequences CANNOT be generated by pushing 1, 2, 3, 4 in order onto a stack and popping at any time?
questions.explanationEn: To pop 4 first, 1, 2, 3, and 4 must all be pushed onto the stack (leaving 3 above 2 above 1). Therefore 3 must be popped before 2; `4, 2, 3, 1` is impossible.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: What is the postfix (Reverse Polish) form of the infix expression `A + B * (C - D) / E`?
questions.explanationEn: Parentheses first: `(C - D)` -> `C D -`. Next `*` and `/` left-to-right: `B * (C D -) / E` -> `B C D - * E /`. Finally `+`: `A B C D - * E / +`.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: In a B-tree of minimum degree `t` (where `t >= 2`), every non-root node must contain at least how many keys?
questions.explanationEn: By definition of a B-tree of minimum degree t, every node other than the root has between `t - 1` and `2t - 1` keys (and between `t` and `2t` children if internal).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: Which traversal of a Binary Search Tree (BST) always visits its keys in non-decreasing (sorted) order?
questions.explanationEn: Inorder traversal visits Left subtree -> Root -> Right subtree. Because all keys in the left subtree are <= root and all keys in the right subtree are >= root, inorder produces sorted order.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about binary trees with `n >= 1` nodes are ALWAYS TRUE?
optionsEn: The first node in Preorder traversal is the same as the last node in Postorder traversal
The number of `NULL` child pointers in a binary tree with `n` nodes is `n + 1`
Every binary tree with `n` nodes has `n - 1` edges
The height of a binary tree with `n` nodes is always at least `floor(log2(n))`
questions.explanationEn: The root is first in preorder and last in postorder (A). Total pointer fields = `2n`; `n - 1` point to children (edges, C), leaving `2n - (n - 1) = n + 1` NULL pointers (B). A binary tree of height `h` has at most `2^(h+1) - 1` nodes, so `h >= floor(log2(n))` (D). All four are true.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
optionsEn: The number of trailing zeros in n
The total number of 1-bits (Hamming weight) in n
The position of the highest set bit in n
questions.explanationEn: Brian Kernighan's trick: `n &= (n - 1)` clears the rightmost 1-bit in each iteration, so the loop executes exactly once per 1-bit in `n`.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: Why are B+ trees preferred over B-trees for database disk indexing?
optionsEn: Internal nodes in a B+ tree store only keys (no record pointers), giving higher fan-out and smaller height, and leaves are linked for fast range scans
B+ trees guarantee O(1) point lookups
B+ trees allow duplicate keys in internal nodes without splitting
B+ trees never require node splits during insertion
questions.explanationEn: Omitting data pointers from internal nodes lets more keys fit per disk block (higher branching factor, fewer disk I/Os), and linked leaf nodes make sequential range queries very fast.

questions.questionTextEn: Given the array `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]` (0-indexed), we convert it into a binary MAX-heap using Floyd's bottom-up `Build-Heap` algorithm (calling `Max-Heapify` from index 2 down to 0). How many total swaps occur?
questions.explanationEn: Idx 2 (val 3, children 6,7): swap 3 & 7 (1 swap) -> `[1, 2, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3]`. Idx 1 (val 2, children 4,5): swap 2 & 5 (1 swap) -> `[1, 5, 7, 4, 2, 6, 3]`. Idx 0 (val 1, children 5,7): swap 1 & 7 (1 swap) -> `[7, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6, 3]`, then 1 at idx 2 swaps with 6 at idx 5 (1 swap) -> `[7, 5, 6, 4, 2, 1, 3]`. Total = 4 swaps.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CS Topic • Programming & Data Structures (Set 1)
questions.questionTextEn: Suppose you need a data structure supporting `Insert` and `Extract-Min` on `n` elements. If you use an unsorted array vs. a binary min-heap, their worst-case complexities for (`Insert`, `Extract-Min`) are respectively:
optionsEn: Unsorted array: (O(n), O(n)); Binary min-heap: (O(log n), O(log n))
Unsorted array: (O(n), O(1)); Binary min-heap: (O(1), O(log n))
Unsorted array: (O(1), O(log n)); Binary min-heap: (O(log n), O(1))
Unsorted array: (O(1), O(n)); Binary min-heap: (O(log n), O(log n))
questions.explanationEn: Appending to an unsorted array is O(1) while scanning for the minimum is O(n). A binary min-heap performs both `Insert` (sift-up) and `Extract-Min` (sift-down) in O(log n).

questions.explanationEn: In a valid BST search for 50, every step narrows the interval `(low, high)` containing 50. A: `(-inf,inf)->(10,inf)->(10,90)->(20,90)->(20,80)->(30,80)->(30,70)->50` (valid). B: valid. D: valid. In C, after 20 we go right to 30, so all subsequent nodes must be > 20; visiting 15 violates BST order.
